segments.title: The scenario and the branch
sections: The Plan That Was A Forecast

cues.text: You wrote a plan before the open. It said the overnight looked firm and the session should go higher.
At 9:41 a.m. price dropped forty points, and you bought it, because the plan said higher.
At 9:52 you bought it again. By 10 a.m. you had been stopped out twice, and you could not say where the plan had told you that you were wrong.
It never said. That was a forecast with a direction in it, and a forecast has no price at which it ends.
The forecast was never wrong. It was never anything, either.
Now, the branch. Your plan is a short list of branches. A branch is one if-then line: if price does a named thing at a named level, you do a named thing, until a named price says you were wrong.
A branch has three parts, always in this order.
One: the thesis. If a behaviour at a zone, and a trigger fires, the price event that says enter now, then a target level. Four slots, each one something you can point to on a chart.
Two: the invalidation. The price, judged on a candle close, at which the thesis is wrong.
Three: the conviction. Strong, moderate or thin.
Levels are written as zones, price bands with two edges, so a branch always knows its far edge, the one on the side away from where price arrives.

Here is a full branch, from a composite plan, invented prices. If price accepts above the pd-high zone, the prior-day high, 21,684 to 21,690, and a Pause N Go fires on the pullback, then prior-week-high is the target.
Accepts means a 5-minute bar closes above the zone. A Pause N Go is two quiet one-minute bars inside the zone, then a close above their high.
Invalidation: a 5-minute close back below 21,684. Conviction: moderate. Nothing in it says the market will go up. It says what you do if it does one particular thing in one particular place.
The rule: every directional line of the plan is a branch: thesis, invalidation, conviction, in that order.
Getting it wrong is a plan that opens with NQ higher, or looking for longs. You are planning the market's actions instead of your own.
The fix: every directional line begins with the word if. A line that begins with anything else is struck through before 9:25 a.m.

segments.title: The level and the trigger
sections: Every Branch Needs A Level And A Trigger

cues.text: A branch has an if clause, and the if clause holds two things. The level says where. The trigger says when.

The level is a zone from your level list, the named prices you mark before the session. Each has a slug, the short name you log it under, like pd-high for the prior-day high or on-low for the overnight low.
The behaviour at the level is a read you can see on a closed bar. Acceptance is one: a 5-minute close beyond the zone within 15 minutes of the first touch.

The trigger is the price event at the level that tells you to enter now, like a Pause N Go, or a level reclaim on a 5-minute close. Order flow, the buying and selling you read bar by bar, can confirm a trigger. It is never the trigger.
Now, what only looks like an if. Six things.
One: an indicator. VWAP, the volume-weighted average price, pivots and moving averages are not locations here.
Two: a day type. Trend day is a label for the whole session, and no price can confirm it at 9:45.
Three: the opening range breaking, the high and low of the session’s first minutes, with no trigger named.
Four: the overnight's direction. The overnight builds levels for your list. It never supplies a direction.
Five: order flow on its own.
Six: a rejection at a range extreme, the top or bottom of the prior range. It can end or cancel a branch, but it carries no entry of its own.
Round numbers are easy to remember. So is a phone number. Neither is a level.
The rule: every branch names a zone from the level list and a trigger from Module 13 that must fire there. A branch missing either is not written.

Getting it wrong is a trigger with no level: buy the first Pause N Go after the open. You are reacting to movement, not to a place, and a trade from the middle of the range has nothing behind its stop.
The fix: write the slug before any other word of the thesis. If you cannot name a slug, the branch does not exist.

segments.title: The invalidation and the nothing case

cues.text: Now, the invalidation. It is a price, judged on a candle close of a stated timeframe, where the thesis is wrong. It sits at or behind the far edge, written before the session and never moved during it.
Show it: a 5-minute close back below 21,684. That line has a number, a timeframe and a direction. Anyone with the chart can say whether it happened, and on which bar.
It is not the stop. The stop is a resting order behind the far edge, placed at entry. The invalidation is the close that tells you the thesis is over, whether or not the stop has filled.
An idea with no written invalidation is No Setup, the journal tag for a trade taken on feel.
The rule: every branch carries one invalidation price with its candle timeframe. No written invalidation means No Setup.
Getting it wrong is out if it starts looking weak. You have not decided where you are wrong, so when the market says no, you argue with it.
The fix: an invalidation line is accepted only with a number and a timeframe. Missing either, it is crossed out.
Now, the nothing case. It is the line of the plan that says where no branch applies, written as a price range with two numbers, ending with the words no trade.
Show it: between 21,562 and 21,684, without acceptance outside it, no trade.
It covers more than the middle of the range. One: any level with no branch attached.
Two: a rejection read with no branch.
Three: a gap open, the session opening outside the prior day’s range, when no gap branch was written.
Doing nothing is a position. It is the only one with no slippage.
The rule: every plan has a nothing case, a price range with two numbers, ending with the words no trade.
Getting it wrong is two branches and no nothing case, then a trade at 10:15 from a level that had no branch. The unplanned space gets filled by impulse.
The fix: say the nothing case aloud before the open. Trade from inside it, and the journal tag is No Setup.

segments.title: The specificity test and the final read

cues.text: Now, the specificity test. After the session, with only the line and the chart, you can mark the bar where it triggered and the price where it ended, without guessing. A line that fails is not a plan line.
Six slots, checked one at a time. One: a level, a slug written as a zone.
Two: a behaviour you can see on a closed bar.
Three: a trigger.
Four: a target that is a level.
Five: an invalidation price with its timeframe.
Six: a conviction.
Here is what the test does to a common line: looking for longs above the prior-day high. It fails on behaviour, trigger, target, invalidation and conviction.
Rewritten: if price accepts above the pd-high zone and a Pause N Go fires on the pullback, then prior-week-high. Invalidation: a 5-minute close below the zone's bottom edge. Conviction: moderate.
Short if it fails at VWAP fails on the level, because VWAP is not a location. Find the slug nearest that price, or put it in the nothing case.
The rule: a branch passes only with all six slots filled. Five of six is not a branch.
Getting it wrong is a plan that always seems to have been right, because every line was loose enough to fit whatever happened. A plan that is never wrong is not brave. It is just vague.
The fix: each evening, mark two bars per branch, where it triggered and where it ended. If you had to guess at either, rewrite it.
Now, the final read. It is the plan as it stands at 9:25 a.m.: one sentence of context, one sentence per branch, and one sentence for the nothing case.
Three things never go in it. One: a day-type label, like trend day.
Two: a directional call, like bullish.
Three: a target for the day's profit. The targets in your plan are levels, not amounts.
The rule: the final read is one paragraph, finished by 9:25 a.m., with no day-type label and no directional call.
Getting it wrong is a plan that runs to a page. You could not decide which branches matter, so you will decide live. The fix: five sentences at most. Cut the branch with the thinnest conviction.

segments.title: Conviction and the worked plan
sections: Worked Case: One Plan, Two Branches And Nothing

cues.text: Now, conviction. A label of strong, moderate or thin on one branch: how much structure stands behind its thesis. Never a direction.
The sheet has no bias field. Each branch carries its own conviction, so a moderate long branch above the range can sit beside a thin short branch below it.
Conviction is counted, not felt, from three checks, one point each. One: the zone holds more than one level from your list.
Two: no other level from your list sits between the zone and the target.
Three: the target is inside the ATR room frame, the normal travel for the day, and no major scheduled release falls in the 9:30 to 11 a.m. window.
Three points is strong. Two is moderate. One or none is thin. Write the reason as one clause. Conviction never changes your size. The grade does, in Module 14.
The rule: each branch carries its own conviction with a one-clause reason, and conviction never stands for a direction.
Getting it wrong is strong on every branch, every day, or a contract added because you felt sure. That is not conviction. It is a habit with a label.
The fix: write each branch backwards. Invalidation first, conviction last. By then you have already written down how you are wrong.
Now, the worked case. A composite plan, invented prices, written by 9:25 a.m. Price is 21,642, inside the prior-day range, 21,520 to 21,690.
Branch 1, written backwards. Invalidation: a 5-minute close back below 21,684.
Then the level and trigger: accept above the pd-high zone, 21,684 to 21,690, and a Pause N Go fires on the pullback.
Target: prior-week-high, 21,790. Conviction: moderate, one level in the zone.
Branch 2 mirrors it. Invalidation: a 5-minute close back above 21,562.
Accept below the pd-val zone, the prior-day value area low, 21,556 to 21,562, and a Pause N Go fires on the pullback.
Target: pd-low, the prior-day low, 21,526. Conviction: moderate, and no trade unless the stop leaves 2 to 1, two of reward for one of risk, because the target is only about 30 points away.
The nothing case: between 21,562 and 21,684, without acceptance outside it, no trade. A gap open above 21,690 or below 21,520, no trade.
That is the final read: four sentences, no day type, no direction. Every line names a price you can see.

cues.text: Take your last five written plans and score each one, a point per line that is true for every branch on it.
One: a level, a slug written as a zone with both edges.
Two: a behaviour you can see on a closed bar.
Three: a named trigger that must fire in the zone.
Four: a target that is a level.
Five: an invalidation price with its candle timeframe.
Six: a conviction, with a one-clause reason.
Seven: a nothing case, a price range with two numbers, ending no trade.
Eight: a final read, one paragraph, no day-type label.
Eight of eight is a plan. Anything less is not yet one.
If any of your five plans missed line five, the trades taken from it were No Setup on the plan’s own terms. The invalidation line is the first thing to fix.
If two or more scored under eight for any other reason, find the line you miss most often and fix that one first.
Getting it wrong is scoring from memory. Memory flatters you. Score from the page.
Now, the assignment. Tonight, write one branch for your next session, backwards.
The invalidation price first. Then the zone and the trigger. Then the target level. Then the conviction, with its reason.
One sentence. That is the whole assignment. It is shorter than the forecast was. It is also the first line you have written that can be wrong.
In one line: a branch, a price that ends it, and a line that says where you do nothing. That is the plan.
Now, where it goes next.
Module 16, the pre-market routine, is where this plan is written each morning. Each branch becomes a line on your sheet, and the final read is spoken in the rehearsal.
Module 17, the session and the close, picks up at 9:30 a.m., with the plan as the only input during the session.
Module 14, trade construction, turns a triggered branch into a trade.
Module 18, journaling and review, is where a branch’s invalidation decides the execution mark, the Pass or Fail written after the exit, and its conviction becomes a field your record can sort by.
